scenarios.title: Read one content record by ID
scenarios.intent: The single most common CMS request: a client fetches one record by its primary key and gets JSON back. Exercises routing, auth check, one indexed point lookup, and JSON marshaling.

scenarios.title: List 50 records (page 1)
scenarios.intent: The list view behind every admin table and public index page. Exercises a bounded, ordered scan plus serializing 50 rows.

scenarios.title: Create one record
scenarios.intent: The write path: validate a body, insert one row, fire lifecycle hooks, return the created record. The scenario that stresses the DB write side and any hook/event machinery.

scenarios.title: Filter by an indexed field
scenarios.intent: A query with a WHERE clause on an indexed column plus pagination, the shape most real API reads take. Catches missing indexes and N+1 relation loading.

scenarios.title: Authenticate (token issuance)
scenarios.intent: Login deliberately runs a slow password hash (bcrypt or argon2), and this scenario measures how gracefully each platform absorbs a burst of logins without the hash starving everything else.

profiles.name: GraphQL Storefront
profiles.tagline: The same catalog over GraphQL, where a page is one request.
profiles.realWorld: A storefront served entirely through GraphQL. The transport's one real advantage over the REST content API is that several root fields travel in one document, so a page that needs three collections of records costs one request instead of three. This profile measures that against the equivalent single-field read. It cannot traverse a relation, because the GraphQL surface exposes the orphan relation column and not the foreign key, so the types carry a denormalized slug instead.

traffic.desc: one root field, the GraphQL equivalent of a REST list
three root fields in one document, which is the only thing this transport does that REST cannot
a wide selection over 50 records, well inside the measured cost ceiling of 1000

rig.repetitions: Every target on 2026-10-26: four repetitions, interleaved (lyeve, strapi, directus, payload, then again), each on a fresh stack. Every kept run started and ended below load 4. One run is set aside under results/raw/excluded: payload 20261026-080758-payload-all, because the load was at or above 4 at its start or end. Each application profile ran three times.
method: Every run brings the target's stack up from nothing, seeds the same 2,020 records from a fixed seed, and tears it down with its volumes afterwards.
Each scenario gets a 10 s discarded warm-up, then a 60 s measured window. The published figure is the median of the runs. The range beneath it is the lowest and highest run.

Before each run the driver waits until no other test workload runs on the machine and the one-minute load average is under 4. The load at the start and end of every run is logged, and a run with either above 4 is excluded.
Image size is the sum of the image's layers from `docker history`, uncompressed. Cold start is `docker start` of the stopped container to the first request the application serves, polled every 50 ms.

LyEve runs in its default production mode behind a proxy that forwards the https scheme. Its free tier limits logins to five per fifteen minutes per address and only a license changes that, so the load scripts reuse one token and S05 reads pending, the rule that has always applied to Strapi.
